title: Load Balancing (Advanced): Application Gateway, Front Door and Traffic Manager
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Explain what a layer 7 reverse proxy adds to load balancing, and what it costs you.
- Describe the parts of an Application Gateway v2 — listeners, rules, backend pools, backend settings and health probes — and how path-based and multi-site routing work.
- Plan a WAF policy: managed rule sets, custom rules, exclusions, Detection and Prevention modes.
- Compare how Azure Front Door, Traffic Manager and the cross-region Load Balancer move users between regions.
- Choose the right service — or combination of services — with a two-question decision tree.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Since Lunch 23 the storefront runs on a scale set across three zones in Indonesia Central, behind the Standard load balancer from Lunch 09. It survived the last sale. Now three new requests land on your desk.

Dewi has moved the product photos into a separate images app and wants www.nusantararetail.co.id/images/... served by it, under the shop's address. Rizky forwards the web server logs: thousands of requests a day contain strings such as ' OR 1=1--, attempts to trick the database into returning every customer. And Ibu Sari has read a news story about a cloud outage that took a whole region offline for an afternoon: "If Jakarta goes down during 12.12, do shoppers in Medan and Makassar just see an error?" Shoppers in eastern Indonesia already complain that product pages load slowly.

The layer 4 load balancer can't help with any of this, because it never reads a request. Today's question: which Azure service should stand in front of the storefront — and when do you need more than one?

Reading

1. Beyond layer 4: what a reverse proxy adds

Azure Load Balancer forwards packets without opening them. That makes it fast and able to carry any protocol, but it is blind: it can't tell a product page from a login form, or a shopper from an attacker. The services in this lunch read the request.

A reverse proxy stands in front of your servers and plays the server's role towards the client. It accepts the client's connection, reads the whole HTTP request, decides where it should go, and sends it on over a second connection of its own. Because it reads every request, a layer 7 proxy can:

- route by content — the host name (www or partners), the URL path (/images/*), headers or query strings;
- terminate TLS — decrypt HTTPS once, with certificates managed in one place, and re-encrypt to the servers if you need to;
- inspect requests with a web application firewall (WAF) and drop attacks before they reach your code;
- change requests and responses — redirect HTTP to HTTPS, rewrite headers, keep a shopper on one server with a cookie;
- cache answers close to users (Front Door).

The trade-offs come from the same design. A proxy speaks HTTP and HTTPS (Application Gateway can also proxy plain TCP and TLS, but HTTP is its home ground), it adds a little latency, and your servers see the proxy's address; the shopper's own address travels in the X-Forwarded-For header.

Azure offers four services that can stand in front of an application, besides the regional load balancer you already know. Two questions sort them: does the traffic speak HTTP(S)? and is it served from one region or several?

| Application Gateway | Azure Front Door | Traffic Manager | Cross-region Load Balancer
Works with | HTTP(S), layer 7 | HTTP(S), layer 7 | DNS, so any protocol | TCP and UDP, layer 4
Scope | one region, inside your virtual network | global, at Microsoft's edge | global | global
In the traffic path? | yes, as a proxy | yes, as a proxy at the edge | no — it only answers DNS queries | yes, passing packets through
When a failure is detected, clients… | stop getting the unhealthy backend at once | keep the same address; the edge picks another origin | move only when their cached DNS answer expires | keep the same address; another region answers
Typical job | path routing, TLS and WAF for one region's apps | one global entry point with caching and WAF | DNS failover or location rules for any endpoint | one static IP for a global TCP or UDP service

2. Application Gateway v2, piece by piece

Azure Application Gateway is a managed reverse proxy that you deploy into your own virtual network, in one region. It needs a dedicated subnet (a /24 is recommended, so it has room to scale), has a static public or private frontend IP address, and is assembled from a handful of parts that you will meet again in the portal and in Lab 27:

Component | What it does | Lab 27 example
Frontend IP | the public and/or private address clients connect to | pip-agw-nusa
Listener | waits on a frontend, port and protocol — optionally for specific host names; an HTTPS listener holds the TLS certificate | HTTP on port 80
Request routing rule | connects one listener to its backend targets; basic (one pool) or path-based; v2 rules have a priority | rule1, path-based
Backend pool | the servers: VM NICs, scale sets, IP addresses or host names such as App Service apps | pool-images with the images app
Backend settings | how to talk to a pool: protocol, port, host name, timeout, cookie affinity, probe | HTTPS on 443, host name taken from the backend
Health probe | regular checks of every backend; members that fail get no requests | probe-app: HTTPS GET /
WAF policy (WAF_v2) | the firewall's rules and mode, attached to the gateway, a listener or a path | waf-nusa in Prevention mode

A rule decides where a request goes; backend settings decide how the gateway delivers it. Three routing features do most of the work:

- Path-based routing. A URL path map lists patterns such as /images/* or /api/*, each with its own pool, plus a default pool for everything else. The gateway forwards the full path unless you rewrite it.
- Multi-site hosting. A basic listener accepts any host name; a multi-site listener matches specific names, wildcards included. That lets www.nusantararetail.co.id and partners.nusantararetail.co.id share one gateway, one IP address and port 443, each with its own rules.
- Redirects and rewrites. Send HTTP to HTTPS, add security headers, or change a URL before the backend sees it.

With TLS termination, the listener holds the certificate — v2 can read it from Azure Key Vault, so renewal happens in one place — and the gateway sees the decrypted request, which the WAF needs. With end-to-end TLS, the backend settings use HTTPS too, so traffic is encrypted again on its way to the servers, and the gateway checks each backend's certificate the way a careful browser would.

Every backend is checked. Without configuration a default probe requests / with the host name 127.0.0.1; a custom probe lets you choose the path, host name, interval and accepted status codes. If every member of a pool fails, the gateway answers 502 Bad Gateway.

There are two production SKUs: Standard_v2, and WAF_v2, which adds the web application firewall. A lighter Basic SKU is in preview at the time of writing, and the original v1 SKUs retired on April 28, 2026. Both v2 SKUs autoscale between a minimum and a maximum instance count you choose, or run at a fixed capacity. In regions with availability zones they spread across at least two zones by default. New instances take minutes rather than seconds, so raise the minimum before a known peak such as 12.12. For Kubernetes traffic Microsoft also offers a separate product, Application Gateway for Containers (Lunch 29).

Warning: App Service behind Application Gateway needs the right host name. App Service runs many apps on shared front ends and picks the app by the request's host name. The gateway forwards the name the shopper typed, and its default probe uses 127.0.0.1 — names App Service doesn't recognise — so the probe fails and shoppers get 502. Either give the app the same custom domain as the listener (the cleanest fix), or set the backend settings to pick the host name from the backend target and add a custom probe that does the same. Lab 27 hits this wall on purpose.

3. The web application firewall: rule sets, modes and scores

A web application firewall looks inside every HTTP request for the patterns of common attacks: SQL injection, cross-site scripting, protocol abuse, malicious bots. On Application Gateway it needs the WAF_v2 SKU and takes its instructions from a WAF policy, a separate Azure resource. You can attach a policy to the whole gateway, to one listener (per-site) or to one path rule (per-URI), so a partner portal can be stricter than the shop.

A policy has four parts:

- Managed rule sets, written and updated by Microsoft. The Default Rule Set (DRS) — version 2.2 is recommended for new policies — builds on the OWASP Core Rule Set and adds Microsoft's own rules. An optional Bot Manager rule set sorts bots into good, bad and unknown.
- Custom rules that you write, evaluated before the managed rules: allow head office's IP range, block a country, or rate-limit the login page.
- Exclusions, which tell the managed rules to ignore one header, cookie or form field that legitimately looks suspicious.
- A mode: Detection only logs what it would have blocked; Prevention blocks it.

DRS uses anomaly scoring. A request that matches a rule isn't rejected on the spot. Each match adds points by severity — 5 for critical, 4 for error, 3 for warning, 2 for notice — and once a request's total reaches the threshold of 5, Prevention mode stops it with HTTP 403 Forbidden. One critical match, such as ' OR 1=1-- in a query string, is enough by itself. A single warning, such as a request addressed to an IP address instead of a host name, is not, which is why Lab 27 can browse the gateway by its IP address. Front Door has WAF policies of its own, built on the same ideas and applied at the edge.

A WAF is a safety net, not a replacement for secure code. Dewi's queries still need parameters, not strings glued together.

Tip: Start every new policy in Detection mode. Send real traffic through it for a few days, ideally including a busy sale day, and read the WAF logs for false positives. Add exclusions or custom rules for them, then switch to Prevention. A policy left in Detection for months protects nothing.

4. Azure Front Door: the front door at Microsoft's edge

Azure Front Door is a global layer 7 service that runs in Microsoft's edge locations — points of presence in metro areas around the world, Jakarta and Singapore among them. Front Door's DNS and network send each shopper to a nearby, healthy edge location. TLS ends there, the WAF inspects the request there, and cached content is served from there. Everything else travels to your origin over Microsoft's own network rather than the public internet.

A Front Door profile has one or more endpoints, each with an azurefd.net host name, plus your custom domains with managed certificates. A route matches domains, path patterns and protocols, and sends requests to an origin group: a set of origins — App Service apps, storage accounts, Application Gateways or any public host name — with a health probe and load-balancing settings. Among the healthy origins, Front Door picks those with the best priority, then the lowest latency, then splits traffic by weight. Rule sets change behaviour per request (redirects, header changes, cache settings), and caching with compression serves static files such as product photos straight from the edge.

Shoppers keep talking to the same edge location, which simply picks another origin, so an origin failover takes effect as soon as the health probes notice — no DNS answer has to change. Front Door comes in two tiers:

Feature | Standard | Premium
Static and dynamic content, caching, compression, rule sets |  |
Custom domains with HTTPS |  |
WAF custom rules, including geo-filtering and rate limits |  |
Microsoft-managed WAF rule set and bot protection | — |
Private Link connection to origins | — |
Built-in reports |  | , plus a WAF report

An origin that anyone can reach directly turns the edge WAF into a suggestion. Lock it down. For App Service, add access restrictions that allow only the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag and require the X-Azure-FDID header to carry your profile's ID — the service tag alone admits every Front Door profile, an attacker's included. With Premium you can reach the origin over Private Link instead, so it needs no public endpoint at all.

Important: Front Door (classic) retires on March 31, 2027, and new classic profiles can no longer be created. Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic) follows on September 30, 2027. Older tutorials that use the az network front-door commands target classic; use az afd for Standard and Premium.

5. Traffic Manager and the cross-region Load Balancer

Azure Traffic Manager steers clients with DNS. You create a profile with a name such as nusa-shop.trafficmanager.net, add endpoints, and point your own domain at the profile with a CNAME record. When a client looks the name up, Traffic Manager chooses a healthy endpoint according to the profile's routing method and answers with that endpoint's name. The client then connects to the endpoint directly. Traffic Manager never touches the traffic, so it works for any protocol — and it can't route by path, end TLS or filter attacks.

Routing method | Returns… | Nusantara Retail example
Priority | the healthy endpoint with the best priority (1 is first) | Indonesia Central; Southeast Asia only if it fails
Weighted | endpoints at random, in proportion to their weights | send 10% of shoppers to a new storefront version
Performance | the endpoint with the lowest network latency from the user's DNS resolver | a future storefront on two continents
Geographic | the endpoint assigned to the region the query comes from | keep Indonesian shoppers on Indonesian infrastructure
MultiValue | several healthy endpoints at once (external IPv4 or IPv6 endpoints only) | a client that retries another address itself
Subnet | the endpoint mapped to the source IP range | head-office staff test a preview version

Endpoints are Azure endpoints (resources such as public IP addresses, or App Service apps on the Standard tier or higher), external endpoints (any host name or IP address, even outside Azure — Lab 27 uses these), or nested endpoints: child profiles, so you can combine methods, for example Geographic on top and Priority inside each geography. Traffic Manager probes every endpoint over HTTP, HTTPS or TCP every 30 seconds, or every 10 seconds with fast probing. After more consecutive failures than you tolerate, the endpoint is marked Degraded and disappears from the answers.

Answering with DNS makes Traffic Manager simple and protocol-neutral, but it brings caveats you must design for:

- Caching. Resolvers and clients keep an answer for the profile's TTL (time to live), and some clients keep it longer. Failover takes roughly detection time plus the TTL plus any extra caching. A low TTL speeds failover but multiplies DNS queries.
- Open connections stay put. A shopper who is already connected keeps talking to the failed endpoint until the connection breaks and the name is looked up again.
- "Location" means the resolver's location. Performance and Geographic routing see the DNS resolver that asked, not the shopper. Someone in Surabaya using a public resolver abroad can be placed wrongly.
- Host names. Each endpoint must accept the name the client asked for, so web apps need your custom domain bound on every endpoint.

For non-HTTP traffic that must fail over faster than DNS allows, Azure Load Balancer has a global tier, the cross-region load balancer. It gives you one static anycast public IP address in front of Standard public load balancers in several regions. It checks the regional load balancers every 5 seconds and sends new connections to a healthy region without any DNS change, and the servers still see the client's own IP address. Its frontend is public only, and the regional load balancers must sit in participating regions. At the time of writing Indonesia Central is not one of them, so check the list before you design around it.

6. Choosing — and combining — for Nusantara Retail

The decision tree needs only the two questions from section 1, plus one follow-up on each side:

Real designs often stack two services, a global one in front of a regional one:

Combination | When it makes sense
Front Door → App Service or Storage | the simplest global web app: edge TLS, caching and WAF, origins locked to your profile
Front Door → Application Gateway in each region | a global entry point plus regional layer 7 routing to private backends in a virtual network
Traffic Manager → Application Gateway in each region | regional gateways with DNS failover, when a slower failover is acceptable
Application Gateway → internal Load Balancer | the gateway serves the web tier; the order API sits behind an internal load balancer
Cross-region Load Balancer → regional public load balancers | a global TCP or UDP service with one static address

Here is the team's design for the next 12.12 sale:

- Front Door Premium answers www.nusantararetail.co.id from the edge: managed certificate, WAF with the managed rule set and bot protection, and product photos cached in edge locations such as Jakarta.
- An Application Gateway in Indonesia Central is the priority 1 origin. It is zone-redundant, sends /images/* to the images app and everything else to the scale set, and accepts only Front Door traffic: an NSG allows the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag, and a custom WAF rule checks X-Azure-FDID. Standard_v2 would do behind Front Door's WAF; the security team chose WAF_v2 for a second layer.
- A smaller copy in Southeast Asia is the priority 2 origin. Customer data must stay in Indonesia, so for now the standby serves the catalogue in browse-only mode; Lunch 28 deals with the orders database.
- The stores' point-of-sale sync, a plain TCP service, gets a Traffic Manager priority profile in front of a public load balancer in each region. A cross-region load balancer would fail over faster, once Indonesia Central joins its list of participating regions.

Pause and think: at 20:00 on 12.12, the storefront in Indonesia Central stops answering. A shopper in Makassar is halfway through checkout. What does she experience if the shop's address points at Traffic Manager with a 60-second TTL — and what if it points at Front Door?

Basic partner: Lunch 09 · Load Balancing (Basic) (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/lunches/09-load-balancing-basic.html) covers Azure Load Balancer, health probes and outbound rules.

Field notes from Stefanus

Always knock on the back door. When a team shows me a new Front Door or Application Gateway with a WAF, my first test is not the front door. I take the origin's own address — the azurewebsites.net name or the server's public IP — and send one request straight to it from a laptop outside the corporate network. If it answers, the WAF only protects the visitors who are polite enough to use the official address; an attacker simply walks around it. I repeat that test after every change, because back doors are rarely left open on purpose: they are reopened by a "temporary" access rule. And if the WAF is still in Detection mode, I ask for the date it moves to Prevention and write that date into the design.

Go further

- Azure Architecture Center: Load balancing options (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/architecture/guide/technology-choices/load-balancing-overview) — Microsoft's own decision tree and the common combinations, in more depth.
- Microsoft Learn: What is Azure Application Gateway v2? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/application-gateway/overview-v2) — SKUs, v2 features and the v1 retirement.
- Microsoft Learn: Comparison between Azure Front Door and Azure Content Delivery Network (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/frontdoor/front-door-cdn-comparison) — what each tier includes, and the retirement dates for the classic services.
- Microsoft Learn: Traffic Manager routing methods (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/traffic-manager/traffic-manager-routing-methods) — all six methods, with the DNS caveats behind each.

quiz.q: Dewi adds the images app (app-nusa-img.azurewebsites.net) to a new backend pool on the gateway. Backend health shows it as Unhealthy and /images/ returns 502, yet the app works when she browses to it directly. What is missing?
quiz.a: Backend settings that pick the host name from the backend target, plus a custom probe that takes its host name from them — or the same custom domain on the app and the listener. Why: App Service chooses the app by host name, and the gateway was sending one it doesn't recognise.

quiz.q: On the first morning of the sale the WAF, in Prevention mode, starts returning 403 for product reviews such as "Drop by the store and select your size". Attack traffic is still being blocked too. What should the team do?
quiz.a: Find the matching rule in the WAF logs and add an exclusion for the review field (or a narrowly scoped custom rule), keeping Prevention mode for everything else. Why: managed rules match patterns, not intentions, so an exclusion removes the false positive without switching off protection.

quiz.q: The storefront uses Traffic Manager priority routing with a 300-second TTL. Indonesia Central fails; the endpoint shows Degraded after about 30 seconds, yet some shoppers still get errors five minutes later. Why, and what would shorten it?
quiz.a: Resolvers and clients keep the cached DNS answer for the TTL, some even longer. Lower the TTL, or use Front Door, whose edge switches origins while clients keep the same address. Why: Traffic Manager only changes future DNS answers; it never moves traffic that already knows where to go.

quiz.q: The stores' point-of-sale devices send sales to head office systems over a custom TCP protocol on port 9000. Pak Budi wants one fixed public IP address that fails over between two regions within seconds. Which service fits?
quiz.a: The cross-region load balancer in front of a Standard public load balancer in each region — if both are participating regions; otherwise Traffic Manager, with DNS-speed failover. Why: Application Gateway and Front Door are built for HTTP(S); only the cross-region load balancer gives TCP one static global address.

quiz.q: Rizky notices SQL-injection attempts sent straight to app-nusa-store.azurewebsites.net, bypassing Front Door and its WAF. The app already allows only the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag. How does he close the gap?
quiz.a: Also require the X-Azure-FDID header to match Nusantara's Front Door profile ID in the access restriction — or use a Private Link origin with Premium. Why: the service tag covers every Front Door profile, including one an attacker creates.

takeaways: A layer 7 reverse proxy reads each request, so it can route by host and path, end TLS and run a WAF; for non-HTTP traffic in one region, Azure Load Balancer (Lunch 09) is still the tool.

Application Gateway v2 (Standard_v2 or WAF_v2; v1 retired April 28, 2026) is regional, zone-redundant and autoscaling: listeners, rules, backend pools, backend settings and probes. App Service backends need the right host name.
A WAF policy combines managed rule sets (DRS 2.2 for new policies), custom rules and exclusions; start in Detection, tune, then switch to Prevention, where anomaly scores of 5 or more get a 403.
Azure Front Door (Standard or Premium; classic retires March 31, 2027) works at Microsoft's edge: TLS, caching, WAF and origin failover without DNS delays. Lock origins to your profile.

Traffic Manager steers any protocol with DNS (six routing methods), but failover waits for TTLs and caches; the cross-region load balancer gives TCP and UDP one anycast IP. Global services often sit in front of regional ones.

lab.title: Protect and route the storefront
lab.text:
What you'll build

Nusantara Retail's storefront and its new images service run as two small App Service apps. You put an Application Gateway (WAF_v2) in front of them that sends /images/* to the images app and everything else to the storefront, and a WAF policy that blocks a SQL-injection attempt with HTTP 403. Then you add a Traffic Manager profile that answers DNS with the storefront first and a standby second, stop the storefront and watch the DNS answer change. Optionally, you put Front Door Standard in front of the storefront to see the global edge.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)).
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. dig and Python are preinstalled.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/27-load-balancing-advanced
source ../common/config.sh
source lab.env          # resource names for this lab, plus helpers: load_hosts, gw_ip, tm_watch
RG=$(rg_name 27)

- Create the starting point — takes about 3–5 minutes. It creates the resource group, the virtual network with the empty subnet snet-agw (10.27.0.0/24, dedicated to the gateway), a Free (F1) App Service plan and two apps with HTTPS only, and deploys the pages in app/:

bash setup.sh
load_hosts              # sets STORE_HOST and IMG_HOST — rerun it whenever you reconnect

Important: This is a lab. An Application Gateway WAF_v2 is billed for every hour it exists, from creation until you delete it, even with no traffic, and the optional Front Door has a base fee while its profile exists. Do the lab in one sitting and run Clean up straight afterwards. The App Service apps use the Free tier. If Cloud Shell disconnects, reconnect, rerun the cd, both source lines and load_hosts; resources keep building in Azure.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–8 (Task 9 is optional)
Challenge | you already know the basics | run bash setup.sh, read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Meet the two apps

Each app labels its own pages, so you can always tell who answered.

curl -s "https://${STORE_HOST}/"        | grep -o "Served by the [A-Z]* app"
curl -s "https://${IMG_HOST}/images/"   | grep -o "Served by the [A-Z]* app"
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n" "https://${STORE_HOST}/images/"

The last command returns 404: the storefront app has no /images/ folder. Only the images app does — the gateway will have to send those requests there.

Checkpoint: Served by the STOREFRONT app, Served by the IMAGES app, and HTTP 404.

Task 2 · Create a WAF policy (Detection first)

A WAF policy is a separate resource that holds the firewall's settings and rule sets; you attach it to the gateway in the next task. Microsoft recommends the Default Rule Set (DRS) 2.2 for new policies (the CLI's default is still 2.1, so you name the version explicitly). Start in Detection mode: matches are logged but nothing is blocked.

az network application-gateway waf-policy create -g "$RG" -n "$WAF_POLICY" -l "$LOCATION" \
  --type Microsoft_DefaultRuleSet --version 2.2 --output none

az network application-gateway waf-policy policy-setting update -g "$RG" --policy-name "$WAF_POLICY" \
  --mode Detection --state Enabled --request-body-check true --output none

az network application-gateway waf-policy show -g "$RG" -n "$WAF_POLICY" \
  --query "{mode:policySettings.mode, state:policySettings.state, ruleSet:managedRules.managedRuleSets[0].ruleSetType, version:managedRules.managedRuleSets[0].ruleSetVersion}" -o table

Checkpoint: Detection, Enabled, Microsoft_DefaultRuleSet, 2.2. (If 2.2 is refused in your region, create the policy with --version 2.1 — see Troubleshooting.)

Task 3 · Create the Application Gateway (5–15 minutes)

The gateway needs a Standard static public IP and its own subnet. You create it with:

- --sku WAF_v2 and the policy from Task 2;
- autoscale between 1 and 2 instances, to keep the lab small (the minimum can also be 0 — pure autoscaling);
- a listener on port 80, and the storefront app as the only member of the default backend pool;
- backend settings that talk HTTPS on port 443 to the app;
- --priority 100 for the routing rule (v2 rules need a priority).

az network public-ip create -g "$RG" -n "$PIP_AGW" -l "$LOCATION" \
  --sku Standard --allocation-method Static --output none

az network application-gateway create -g "$RG" -n "$AGW" -l "$LOCATION" \
  --sku WAF_v2 --min-capacity 1 --max-capacity 2 \
  --vnet-name "$VNET" --subnet "$SUBNET_AGW" \
  --public-ip-address "$PIP_AGW" --waf-policy "$WAF_POLICY" \
  --frontend-port 80 --http-settings-protocol Https --http-settings-port 443 \
  --servers "$STORE_HOST" --priority 100 --output none

While it builds, reread sections 2 and 3 of the lunch. The command creates default components you will reuse: appGatewayFrontendIP, appGatewayHttpListener, appGatewayBackendPool (the storefront), appGatewayBackendHttpSettings and the rule rule1. In regions with availability zones the gateway is spread across zones automatically.

Now try it:

GW_IP=$(gw_ip); echo "$GW_IP"
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n" "http://${GW_IP}/"

Checkpoint: az network application-gateway show -g "$RG" -n "$AGW" --query "{sku:sku.name, state:operationalState}" -o table shows WAF_v2 and Running — and the request fails, typically with HTTP 502 (Bad Gateway). That is expected; Task 4 explains why.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Open agw-nusa and look at Backend health: the storefront is Unhealthy, and the details mention the host name or the certificate's common name. The portal also lets you browse every component you just created: Listeners, Rules, Backend pools, Backend settings, Health probes, and the linked Web application firewall policy.

Task 4 · Teach the gateway to talk to App Service

App Service hosts many customers' apps on shared front ends and finds the right app by the host name in each request. The gateway forwards the host name the client used (an IP address here), and its default health probe uses 127.0.0.1. App Service recognises neither, and the HTTPS certificate (*.azurewebsites.net) doesn't match them either — so the backend is marked unhealthy and shoppers get 502.

The fix: make the backend settings pick the host name from the backend target (each app's own *.azurewebsites.net name), and add a custom probe that takes its host name from those settings.

az network application-gateway probe create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$AGW" -n "$PROBE_AGW" \
  --protocol Https --path / --host-name-from-http-settings true \
  --interval 30 --timeout 30 --threshold 3 --output none

az network application-gateway http-settings update -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$AGW" \
  -n appGatewayBackendHttpSettings --host-name-from-backend-pool true --probe "$PROBE_AGW" --output none

az network application-gateway show-backend-health -g "$RG" -n "$AGW" \
  --query "backendAddressPools[].backendHttpSettingsCollection[].servers[].{address:address, health:health}" -o table

curl -s "http://${GW_IP}/" | grep -o "Served by the [A-Z]* app"

Each application-gateway ... create/update command updates the whole gateway, so expect a minute or two per command.

Checkpoint: the storefront host shows Healthy, and the gateway now returns Served by the STOREFRONT app. In production you would rather put the same custom domain on the gateway and the app, so the host name never has to change (the lunch explains why).

Task 5 · Route /images/* to the images app

Add a second backend pool for the images app, a URL path map that sends /images/* there (everything else goes to the default pool), and switch rule1 from Basic to PathBasedRouting. Quote "/images/*" so the shell does not expand the asterisk.

az network application-gateway address-pool create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$AGW" -n "$POOL_IMG" \
  --servers "$IMG_HOST" --output none

az network application-gateway url-path-map create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$AGW" -n "$PATH_MAP" \
  --rule-name images --paths "/images/*" \
  --address-pool "$POOL_IMG" --http-settings appGatewayBackendHttpSettings \
  --default-address-pool appGatewayBackendPool --default-http-settings appGatewayBackendHttpSettings \
  --output none

az network application-gateway rule update -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$AGW" -n rule1 \
  --rule-type PathBasedRouting --url-path-map "$PATH_MAP" --output none

One backend settings object serves both pools: because it picks the host name from each pool's target, every app receives its own name. Test both paths and the image itself:

curl -s "http://${GW_IP}/"        | grep -o "Served by the [A-Z]* app"
curl -s "http://${GW_IP}/images/" | grep -o "Served by the [A-Z]* app"
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code} %{content_type}\n" "http://${GW_IP}/images/batik.svg"

Checkpoint: / is served by the STOREFRONT app, /images/ by the IMAGES app, and the SVG returns HTTP 200 image/svg+xml. Open http://<gateway IP>/ in a browser and click the images link. The gateway forwards the full path, which is why the images app keeps its pages in an images folder.

Task 6 · Switch the WAF to Prevention and block an attack

Send a classic SQL-injection probe (?id=1' OR 1=1--, URL-encoded) while the policy is still in Detection mode:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n" "http://${GW_IP}/?id=1%27%20OR%201%3D1--"

You get HTTP 200: in Detection mode the WAF only logs the match. Now switch to Prevention:

az network application-gateway waf-policy policy-setting update -g "$RG" --policy-name "$WAF_POLICY" \
  --mode Prevention --state Enabled --request-body-check true --output none

Wait a minute or two for the change to reach the gateway, then send the same request — and a normal one:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "attack: HTTP %{http_code}\n" "http://${GW_IP}/?id=1%27%20OR%201%3D1--"
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "normal: HTTP %{http_code}\n" "http://${GW_IP}/?id=42"

Checkpoint: attack: HTTP 403 and normal: HTTP 200. The SQL-injection rule is critical (anomaly score 5), which reaches the blocking threshold of 5 on its own; the storefront never sees the request.

Task 7 · A Traffic Manager profile with priority routing

Traffic Manager answers DNS queries; it never touches the HTTP traffic. Create a Priority profile with a 30-second TTL and fast HTTPS health checks (every 10 seconds, degraded after 3 failures in a row), then add both apps as external endpoints. (Free-tier apps can't be Azure endpoints; that needs the Standard tier or higher.)

az network traffic-manager profile create -g "$RG" -n "$TM_PROFILE" \
  --routing-method Priority --unique-dns-name "$TM_DNS" --ttl 30 \
  --protocol HTTPS --port 443 --path "/" --interval 10 --timeout 9 --max-failures 2 --output none

az network traffic-manager endpoint create -g "$RG" --profile-name "$TM_PROFILE" -n ep-store \
  --type externalEndpoints --target "$STORE_HOST" --priority 1 --endpoint-status Enabled --output none

az network traffic-manager endpoint create -g "$RG" --profile-name "$TM_PROFILE" -n ep-images \
  --type externalEndpoints --target "$IMG_HOST" --priority 2 --endpoint-status Enabled --output none

Here the images app plays the standby copy of the storefront; in production it would be the same storefront in a second region. Give the probes a minute, then look at endpoint health and at the DNS answer:

tm_watch 3
dig +noall +answer "${TM_DNS}.trafficmanager.net"

Checkpoint: both endpoints are Online, and the first DNS record is a CNAME to app-nusa-store-…, with a TTL of 30 seconds or less. Traffic Manager handed out a name; the client connects to the app directly.

Try curl -s -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n" "https://${TM_DNS}.trafficmanager.net/": the TLS check fails, and over plain HTTP App Service answers with a not found page. The app doesn't know the trafficmanager.net name. In production both apps would carry the same custom domain (Basic tier or higher), and that domain would point at Traffic Manager.

Task 8 · Fail over through DNS

Stop the storefront app — the equivalent of losing the primary site — and watch Traffic Manager react:

az webapp stop -g "$RG" -n "$APP_STORE"
tm_watch 9          # about 90 seconds

Within about a minute the stopped app fails three health checks in a row (ep-store:Degraded), and the DNS answer switches to app-nusa-img-…. Any resolver that cached the old answer keeps it for up to the 30-second TTL; some clients cache longer. Failover time is roughly detection plus TTL plus client caching. Now recover:

az webapp start -g "$RG" -n "$APP_STORE"
tm_watch 9

Checkpoint: you saw ep-store go Degraded and the answer move to the images app, then both return to Online with the storefront first again.

Task 9 (optional) · Put Front Door Standard in front of the storefront

Front Door takes about 15 minutes, mostly waiting for its configuration to reach the edge. Skip it if you are short of time or budget.

az provider register -n Microsoft.Cdn --wait

az afd profile create -g "$RG" --profile-name "$AFD_PROFILE" --sku Standard_AzureFrontDoor --output none
az afd endpoint create -g "$RG" --profile-name "$AFD_PROFILE" --endpoint-name "$AFD_ENDPOINT" \
  --enabled-state Enabled --output none
az afd origin-group create -g "$RG" --profile-name "$AFD_PROFILE" --origin-group-name og-storefront \
  --probe-request-type GET --probe-protocol Https --probe-interval-in-seconds 60 --probe-path / \
  --sample-size 4 --successful-samples-required 3 --additional-latency-in-milliseconds 50 --output none
az afd origin create -g "$RG" --profile-name "$AFD_PROFILE" --origin-group-name og-storefront \
  --origin-name storefront --host-name "$STORE_HOST" --origin-host-header "$STORE_HOST" \
  --priority 1 --weight 1000 --enabled-state Enabled --http-port 80 --https-port 443 --output none
az afd route create -g "$RG" --profile-name "$AFD_PROFILE" --endpoint-name "$AFD_ENDPOINT" \
  --route-name route-default --origin-group og-storefront --supported-protocols Http Https \
  --forwarding-protocol HttpsOnly --https-redirect Enabled --link-to-default-domain Enabled --output none

AFD_HOST=$(az afd endpoint show -g "$RG" --profile-name "$AFD_PROFILE" --endpoint-name "$AFD_ENDPOINT" --query hostName -o tsv)
echo "https://${AFD_HOST}/"

Note --origin-host-header: like Application Gateway, Front Door must send the app's own host name. Retry curl -s "https://${AFD_HOST}/" | grep -o "Served by the [A-Z]* app" every minute or two. Until the configuration has propagated you get an error page from Front Door, not from your app.

Checkpoint: the Front Door host name (…azurefd.net) returns Served by the STOREFRONT app, over HTTPS with Microsoft's certificate, from the edge location nearest to your Cloud Shell.

Break it and fix it

Dewi "tidies up" the path rule and drops one letter:

az network application-gateway url-path-map rule update -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$AGW" \
  --path-map-name "$PATH_MAP" -n images --paths "/image/*" --output none
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n" "http://${GW_IP}/images/"

Symptom: /images/ now returns HTTP 404, although both apps are healthy and the backend health page is all green.

Hint

Ask the gateway how it routes: az network application-gateway url-path-map show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$AGW" -n "$PATH_MAP" --query "pathRules[].{name:name, paths:join(',', paths)}" -o table. A request that matches no path rule goes to the default pool, the storefront app, which has no /images/ folder, so the 404 comes from the storefront app.

Fix

az network application-gateway url-path-map rule update -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$AGW" \
  --path-map-name "$PATH_MAP" -n images --paths "/images/*" --output none
curl -s "http://${GW_IP}/images/" | grep -o "Served by the [A-Z]* app"

Lesson: "healthy backends, wrong page" usually means a routing rule, not a server, is to blame.

Verify your work

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit. Run it after the apps are started again (Task 8) and at least two minutes after switching the WAF to Prevention.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

This deletes the resource group rg-lunch27-<suffix> — gateway, WAF policy, public IP, Traffic Manager profile, optional Front Door, plan and apps — and the local out folder. Nothing lives outside the group. The gateway can take 5–10 minutes to disappear; deletion continues in the background.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
setup.sh: az appservice plan create refuses the Free tier (for example a quota or "not available" message) | Free plans are limited per subscription or region | APP_SKU=B1 bash setup.sh (a small hourly charge), or use another region
setup.sh notes that an app did not show its page yet | first start of a Free-tier app can be slow | wait a minute, then curl -s "https://${STORE_HOST}/"; rerun bash setup.sh to redeploy
waf-policy create rejects --version 2.2 | the rule set version isn't offered to you yet | create it with --version 2.1 (still supported)
application-gateway create fails with an error about the request routing rule priority | v2 rules need a priority | include --priority 100
application-gateway create fails because the subnet is in use or too small | the subnet must be dedicated to Application Gateway | use the empty snet-agw (/24) that setup.sh created
HTTP 502 from the gateway | the backend is unhealthy — almost always the host name for App Service | Task 4; check show-backend-health
HTTP 404 for /images/ through the gateway | path rule missing or misspelt, or rule1 still Basic | az network application-gateway rule show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$AGW" -n rule1 --query ruleType; Task 5
rule update to PathBasedRouting fails | the CLI refused the change on your version | portal: agw-nusa › Rules › rule1 › Backend targets › Add multiple targets to create a path-based rule (/images/* → pool-images)
The attack still returns 200 after switching to Prevention | the policy change hasn't reached the gateway yet | wait two minutes and retry; confirm with waf-policy show ... --query policySettings.mode
Normal pages return 403 | a WAF false positive on your own traffic | switch to Detection, find the rule ID in the WAF logs, add an exclusion, then return to Prevention
Traffic Manager endpoints stay Degraded | probe can't get 200 (app stopped, or HTTP probing an HTTPS-only app) | start the apps; the profile must probe HTTPS on 443
dig still shows the old app after the failover | DNS caching | wait for the TTL (30 s) and retry
Front Door returns an error page | configuration still propagating to the edge | wait several minutes and retry

Stretch goals

- Front Door failover without DNS: add the images app as a second origin (--priority 2) to og-storefront, stop the storefront and watch Front Door switch, with no TTL to wait for.
- Read the WAF logs: send the gateway's diagnostic logs to a Log Analytics workspace and find your blocked request in the firewall log (Lunch 30 teaches the query language).
- A custom WAF rule: block requests whose User-Agent contains sqlmap, or rate-limit a path, with az network application-gateway waf-policy custom-rule create.
- Lock the apps down: add App Service access restrictions so the apps accept traffic only from the gateway (its public IP, or its subnet through a service endpoint).
- Compare with the portal: rebuild the path rule in Rules › Add a routing rule and notice how the portal groups listener, backend targets and backend settings.

Challenge brief

Run bash setup.sh, then build the following, any way you like (portal, CLI, Bicep), using the names from lab.env:

1. A WAF policy waf-nusa, enabled in Prevention mode, with a Microsoft Default Rule Set.
2. An Application Gateway agw-nusa, SKU WAF_v2, at most 2 instances, using waf-nusa, listening on HTTP port 80 on the public IP pip-agw-nusa, in subnet snet-agw.
3. Backend settings over HTTPS 443 that pick the host name from the backend target, with a custom probe that picks its host name from those settings.
4. Path-based routing: /images/* → the images app; everything else → the storefront app.
5. A SQL-injection probe through the gateway (/?id=1' OR 1=1--) is answered with 403, while / and /images/ work.
6. A Traffic Manager profile tm-nusa (DNS name nusa-shop-<suffix>) with Priority routing, HTTPS health checks and two external endpoints: the storefront app (priority 1) and the images app (priority 2).

Then run bash verify.sh. Stuck? Peek at solution.sh or switch to Guided mode.
